posts.body_html:
My cobras are really doing well this season!! Looking at the size and amount of new growth compared to the previous year's is simply amazing. Last year, most of these were all one growth point and pretty small, mostly 6-8", tallest was 10". When the live sphag got going, I could barely make them out except for their heads peeking through. Old growth from the previous year is visible by their decaying heads and was half the height. However, there must have been a lot of stolon growth becuase one pot that was mostly barren except one mother plant is now overgrown with a dozen babies and new growth is popping up everywhere. All I can say is that mine need to sit in water to be happy. Most are in 3"+ and one 12" pot is submerged to the crown. I don't shuffle them around when we have heat waves, nor do I water with cool water. A little peeved that I had aphids from my goji plants feeding on them earlier which deformed many growing pitchers but hopefully they have moved onto tastier morsels. Anywho, it is a really rewarding sight after the massacre I had 2 years ago.

They are finally HAPPY. Well, at least for now.

posts.body_html:
I've grown Darlingtonia a couple ways, always with a shallow water layer near the root tips. One method was to reverse dormancy and refrigerate the plant in Live sphagnum fro about June–Oct. 1. Then when nights were cool and my basement stayed cool, the plants were grown under florescent light, lots of it. the plants routinely got 20 inches tall.

When I moved into a rustic cabin, I had to give them away. Now, I'm working on a more heat tolerant strain. Only a couple plants survived out of hundreds of seedlings. A friend used a thermometer to collect seed, years ago, from plants growing in the warmest soil/water. So far, these have survived rank heat and humidity in Virginia, in a greenhouse! They grow super slowly and the plan is to treat them with preventative fungicide and move the two seedlings to a temperature controlled lab, where they'll be much cooler.

Then, IF seed can be produced, it'll go through the same selective heat pressure as the parents.

I always aerate the media and water when watering, but it's best to avoid wetting the crown. The petioles can collect water and provide a great spot for pathogens to get started.

posts.body_html: A picture from 3 years ago, I lost most of these during a heat wave unfortunately! Only a few stragglers still hanging on today, you really either need a greenhouse in my climate or you need to live in a cooler climate to grow these long term. They're quite heat tolerant as smaller plants, but once they get big, soil temps above 75F for a few days can wipe them out. This might only be true in small pots or shallow trays, maybe big bogs with large volumes of soil will keep them buffered enough from temperature swings. Will probably experiment more in the future, but for now, I'm taking a break from Darlingtonia.

posts.body_html: Been struggling with darlingtonia until now, been very cold this spring so it's not so easy to screw them up! If you keep the soil temperatures 75F or below, you're in the clear, anything above that is playing russian roulette. Air temperatures are irrelevant: it can be 110F out there and they'll still do fine if the soil stays cool. Pics taken 6/8/23:
